design_detail: Prospective cohort analysis of the Danish Diet, Cancer and Health study: 55,917 Danish-born people (26,696 men, 29,221 women) aged 50–64 when invited (December 1993 to May 1997), questioned and examined at baseline, and followed in national registers to 31 December 2011 (median 14.9 years; 831,285 person-years) for a first register diagnosis of alcoholic cirrhosis (257 men, 85 women). All exposures come from one baseline questionnaire: weekly amount by beverage converted to 12-g standard drinks, drinking frequency (days a week), recalled average weekly intake at ages 20–29, 30–39, 40–49 and 50–59, and the wine share of weekly intake. Sex-stratified Cox models with age as the time axis, adjusted for smoking, education and waist circumference, test three stated hypotheses: daily drinking carries more risk than less frequent drinking, current intake matters more than lifetime intake, and wine carries less risk than beer and liquor. Read from the online-first (article in press) PDF, pages 1–7; the printed article is J Hepatol 2015;62:1061–1067.
can_establish: Within this middle-aged Danish cohort, how the incidence of a register diagnosis of alcoholic cirrhosis over about 15 years varied with self-reported baseline amount, drinking frequency, recalled intake in earlier decades and wine share, after adjustment for smoking, education and waist circumference.
cannot_establish: That drinking frequency or wine affects cirrhosis risk beyond the amount drunk (frequency and amount are highly correlated and the authors say they cannot be separated, and wine share may stand for unmeasured habits such as drinking with meals); that cutting down removes the risk of past heavy drinking (intake was measured once, earlier decades only by recall at age 50–64, and no change in drinking was observed); that lifetime abstainers have no risk (the outcome presupposes drinking, and fewer than two cases would have been expected among them); or what holds for women (85 cases) and for heavy drinking occasions (not measured).

sample.recruitment: Community cohort. From December 1993 to May 1997, 160,725 Danish-born men and women aged 50 to 64 without a previous cancer diagnosis were invited to the Diet, Cancer and Health study, designed to study diet, lifestyle and cancer; 27,178 men and 29,875 women took part (response 35%). Participants completed a food-frequency questionnaire, a lifestyle questionnaire (alcohol, smoking, physical activity, education) and a brief physical examination with waist circumference (Materials and methods › Study population, p. 2 of the online-first PDF).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Excluded: alcoholic cirrhosis diagnosed before baseline (86); missing information on alcohol amount (105), smoking (27), education (27) or waist circumference (50); conflicting answers on alcohol amount and frequency (236) or on smoking status and tobacco use (7) (p. 2).
sample.demographics: Median age 55 to 60 years across drinking-frequency groups. Men drinking daily: median 26 drinks a week (5th–95th percentile 9.4–60), 47% smokers, 33% with 7 years of schooling or less; men drinking 2–4 days a week: 8.9 drinks (3.6–13), 34% smokers. Women drinking daily: 19 drinks a week (7.3–40), 43% smokers; women drinking 2–4 days a week: 6.6 (3.0–19), 27% smokers (Table 1, p. 3).
sample.attrition: Register follow-up from baseline to diagnosis of alcoholic cirrhosis (342), emigration (337), loss to follow-up (2), death from other causes (8132) or 31 December 2011; 831,285 person-years; median 14.9 years (14.6 men, 15.1 women) (Follow-up, p. 2; Results, 1st paragraph, p. 2). Deaths from other causes were censored.
sample.selection_effects: Only 35% of those invited took part, and the authors note that participants may live more healthily than non-participants and that women's incidence of alcoholic cirrhosis was somewhat lower than national data would predict (Strengths and limitations, 1st paragraph, p. 6). Lifetime abstainers are very few (63 men, 265 women). Current abstainers include former heavy drinkers: their median lifetime average was 18 drinks a week in men, against 15 in daily drinkers, and 55% of them smoked (Table 1, p. 3). The listed exclusions sum to 538, but 1136 of the 57,053 participants are missing from the analysed cohort (editors' arithmetic; see reporting issues).

exposure.measurement: Self-report at baseline only: average weekly amount of beer (light, regular and strong, in 330 ml bottles), wine (125 ml glasses) and liquor (30 ml drinks), converted to standard drinks of 12 g ethanol; frequency in seven categories (never, less than one day a month, one to three days a month, once a week, two to four, five to six days a week, daily); recalled average weekly intake at ages 20–29, 30–39, 40–49 and 50–59, summed to lifetime drinks and a lifetime average since age 20 (Information on alcohol consumption, p. 2). No repeated measurement during follow-up and no biological verification.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Standard drink = 12 g ethanol. Amount in drinks a week, categorized <14 (reference), 14–28, 28–42, 42–56, 56–70 and >70 in men, with women above 42 grouped (Fig. 1, p. 3). Frequency analysed as <1, 1, 2–4 (reference), 5–6 and 7 days a week (Table 2, p. 4). Wine share of weekly intake <1%, 1–15%, 15–50% and 50–100% (Fig. 2, p. 5). Frequency was strongly correlated with amount: Spearman r = 0.77 in men, 0.85 in women (Results, 1st paragraph, p. 2). Binge drinking could not be examined (Introduction, last paragraph, p. 2).
exposure.polysubstance: Smoking measured and adjusted (never, former, under 10 g tobacco a day, over 10 g a day). Other drug use not measured. Hepatitis C status not available; the authors call this a minor limitation because of its low prevalence in Denmark (p. 6).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable. Lifetime abstainers (no alcohol over lifetime or at baseline) and current abstainers (drank in the past but not at baseline) were kept apart from drinkers (Statistical analysis, 2nd paragraph, p. 2).

comparison.controls: The reference differs by analysis: drinkers of fewer than 14 drinks a week for amount (Fig. 1); people drinking two to four days a week for frequency (Table 2); men drinking fewer than 14 drinks a week who took 50–100% of it as wine for beverage type (Fig. 2); per-drink hazard ratios for the life-period analyses (Tables 3 and 4). Lifetime abstainers had no cases and could not serve as a reference.
comparison.matching: None. Adjustment for smoking, length of education (7 years or less, 8–10, 11 or more) and waist circumference (WHO categories), with age as the time axis; all analyses stratified by sex (Statistical analysis, 1st and 6th paragraphs, p. 2).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Hepatitis B and C, diabetes, diet and physical activity (both measured in the cohort but not used as covariates), heavy drinking occasions, drinking with meals (the authors' explanation for part of the wine finding, p. 6), drinking before age 20, and socioeconomic position beyond education were not adjusted for.

outcomes.instruments: First diagnosis of alcoholic cirrhosis (ICD-8 571.0; ICD-10 K70.3) in the Danish National Patient Register (all somatic admissions since 1977, outpatient contacts since 1995) or the Danish Register of Causes of Death, linked by personal identifier (Follow-up, p. 2). A supplementary combined outcome added unspecified cirrhosis (ICD-8 571.9, 456.0, 785.3; ICD-10 I85.0, I85.9, K74.6, R18.9): 393 men and 229 women (Statistical analysis, 7th paragraph, p. 2; Results, p. 5). Deaths were 11% of cases (p. 6).
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors cite earlier work for a high validity of the register diagnosis (p. 2, refs 21 and 22); no validation within this cohort is reported. Classifying a cirrhosis as alcoholic depends on clinicians knowing that the person drank, so the outcome definition is itself tied to the exposure (editors' observation).
outcomes.operationalization: Hazard ratios from Cox proportional hazards models, proportional hazards checked by parallel stratified survival curves (no violation found). Trend tests across frequency categories exclude abstainers; interaction tests by nested likelihood-ratio tests and by comparing per-drink slopes across frequency groups (Statistical analysis, p. 2).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Two outcomes (alcoholic cirrhosis; alcoholic or unspecified cirrhosis in the supplement), but each of three hypotheses was tested in both sexes with several adjustment levels and parametrizations (categories, per-drink slopes, trend and interaction tests).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable: diagnoses come from routine care registers, independent of the study.

analysis.effect_sizes: Standard drink = 12 g; adjusted for smoking, education and waist circumference, age as time axis. Amount against drinkers of fewer than 14 drinks a week: 14–28 drinks a week, men HR 2.33 (95% CI 1.52–3.58), women 3.49 (2.00–6.12); 28–42 drinks, men 6.98 (4.65–10.5), women 16.2 (9.16–28.7); current abstainers, men 7.58 (3.39–16.9), women 3.21 (0.77–13.4) (p. 3). Frequency against 2–4 days a week, fully adjusted (Table 2, p. 4): men daily 3.65 (2.39–5.55), 5–6 days 1.43 (0.84–2.43), 1 day 1.30 (0.59–2.87), <1 day 1.34 (0.67–2.67), current abstainers 10.0 (4.32–23.0), trend P < 0.001; women daily 1.73 (0.85–3.52), 5–6 days 2.30 (1.14–4.67), 1 day 0.81 (0.29–2.24), <1 day 1.45 (0.71–2.96), current abstainers 4.03 (0.91–17.8), trend P = 0.14. Men's daily HR was 8.29 (5.52–12.4) adjusted for age only and 4.83 (3.20–7.29) with amount added. Per additional weekly drink (Table 3, p. 4): men 1.02 (<1 day a week) to 1.05 (daily); women 1.09 (<1 day) to 1.05 (daily); interaction P < 0.0001 and P = 0.0007. Life periods (Table 4, p. 5): after adjustment for baseline intake, men 20–29 1.00 (0.99–1.01), 30–39 0.99 (0.98–1.01), 40–49 1.01 (1.00–1.02), 50–59 1.03 (1.02–1.03); lifetime average adjusted for baseline 1.03 (1.02–1.03) in men and 1.03 (1.01–1.06) in women. Wine, men at 14–28 drinks a week against men drinking <14 a week mostly as wine: <1% wine 7.47 (1.68–33.12), 1–15% 3.12 (1.53–6.39), 50–100% 1.69 (0.79–3.65); wine share × amount interaction P = 0.63 (p. 5). Editors' calculation of crude incidence per 100,000 person-years from Table 2: men daily 165, 5–6 days 45, 2–4 days 20, current abstainers 154; women daily 51, 5–6 days 36, 2–4 days 10.
analysis.covariates: Age (time axis), smoking (four categories), length of education (three categories), waist circumference (three categories), by sex; amount added for the frequency analyses; other beverages controlled in the beverage-specific models (Supplementary Table 6, not on file); baseline intake added in the life-period models. In the main frequency analysis (Table 2) amount entered as a continuous term (Statistical analysis, 4th paragraph, p. 2); because risk rises steeply across amount categories (Fig. 1), this adjustment may leave confounding by amount in the daily-drinking hazard ratios (editors' reading).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; the three hypotheses are stated in the Introduction (p. 2).
analysis.selective_reporting: Estimates for the heaviest drinkers (men 42–56, 56–70 and over 70 drinks a week; women over 42) are shown only in Fig. 1, and the wine-share estimates other than three quoted in the text only in Fig. 2, which has no confidence intervals. The amount-by-frequency table that the authors say makes frequency and amount hard to separate (Supplementary Table 5), the beverage-specific models (Supplementary Table 6) and all analyses of the combined cirrhosis outcome (Supplementary Tables 2A–6A, Fig. 2A) are online supplements, not on file. The beverage analysis was not done in women because there were few cases.
analysis.power: Not reported. With 85 cases in women (30 among daily drinkers) the authors say firm conclusions for women are not possible (p. 6); with 0 cases in 4846 person-years among lifetime abstainers, their risk cannot be estimated (editors' observation).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Risk of a register diagnosis of alcoholic cirrhosis rose steeply with the amount drunk in both sexes. In men, daily drinking went with about 3.7 times the hazard of drinking two to four days a week after adjustment for amount and confounders; adjustment for amount alone more than halved the age-adjusted estimate (8.29 to 4.83), and the authors could not separate frequency from amount. In women, frequency showed no trend: the highest hazard was at five to six days a week and daily drinking was not significantly raised. Recalled intake in the twenties and thirties added nothing once current intake was known, but the lifetime average still did (1.03 per weekly drink in both sexes). Men drinking 14–28 drinks a week mostly as wine had a lower hazard than those drinking little wine, with wide, overlapping intervals and no significant interaction.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says daily drinking was associated with an increased risk in men, that recent rather than earlier consumption was associated with risk, that wine might be associated with a lower risk, and that results were in general similar for women (p. 1). The discussion goes further: the results are said to confirm that daily drinking increases the risk (p. 6); the conclusions say daily drinking appears to raise risk regardless of amount, at least in men (p. 6); and the implications say there is gain in cutting down whatever the lifetime intake and that “daily drinkers should be advised to drink less frequently” (p. 6). Gaps: (1) causal and advisory language on frequency, although the authors themselves state that frequency and amount could not be disentangled (p. 4) and residual confounding by a self-reported amount is likely; (2) the women's frequency results do not resemble the men's (trend P = 0.14; highest hazard at five to six days; steepest per-drink slope in the least frequent drinkers); (3) 'recent rather than lifetime' overstates Table 4, where the lifetime average remains associated after adjustment for baseline, and where the recent periods overlap the baseline measure while earlier periods rest on recall over decades; (4) no participant was observed cutting down; (5) 'no risk among lifetime abstainers' is stated as a finding (pp. 1, 6) although an alcoholic-cirrhosis diagnosis presupposes drinking and fewer than two cases would have been expected among them.

timeline.event: Becker et al. (Hepatology), a Danish population study of alcohol intake, sex, age and liver-disease risk (this paper's ref 21), one of the 17 studies of the Rehm et al. (2010) meta-analysis.

Becker et al. (Hepatology): lower risk of alcohol-induced cirrhosis in wine drinkers, which this study agrees with; Pelletier et al. (Alcohol Alcohol) found no lower risk with wine in heavy drinkers, which it conflicts with (refs 18 and 19, p. 6).
Kamper-Jørgensen et al. (J Hepatol): dose–response or threshold for cirrhosis (ref 7), cited for earlier findings on frequency, recent intake and beverage type (pp. 1, 6).

Hatton et al. (Addiction), drinking patterns and lifetime drinking history in people with alcohol-related liver disease (ref 12): among the earlier studies in clinical samples that compared daily with episodic drinking (p. 6).
Rehm et al. meta-analysis: different dose–response for cirrhosis morbidity and mortality; this cohort, with deaths only 11% of its cases, could not separate the two (p. 6; card sc_rehm_2010).
This study: first comparison of daily drinking with drinking five or six days a week in a general population, by the authors' account (p. 6).

Roerecke et al. (Am J Gastroenterol), dose–response meta-analysis of alcohol and cirrhosis (card sc_roerecke_2019): this cohort is one of its nine studies (its Table 1), although the cohort's men contribute no estimate to its main analysis. It reports daily-drinking ratios for this cohort at the same weekly intake (men 2.25, women 1.28) that are not in this paper's main text, which gives 3.65 and 1.73 (Table 2, fully adjusted). Its Table 1 lists this cohort with 393 men and 229 women, the counts of this paper's supplementary combined outcome of alcoholic or unspecified cirrhosis (Statistical analysis, 7th paragraph, p. 2; pp. 5–6), so its figures probably come from that analysis (editors' reading; supplement not on file).

replication.where_it_stands: The steep amount gradient agrees with the meta-analyses (sc_rehm_2010). The association of daily drinking with alcoholic cirrhosis in men agrees in direction with earlier clinical studies the authors cite, but in this cohort it cannot be separated from amount, and in women it was not found; the wine finding agrees with one earlier Danish study and conflicts with studies of heavy drinkers. The Diet, Cancer and Health cohort is not among the 17 studies of Rehm et al. (2010), so the two are independent; the 2019 meta-analysis (Roerecke et al.) includes this cohort, so the two are not independent and are counted once when cited together.

funding.funder: Not reported. The authors declare that they have nothing to disclose regarding funding or conflict of interest with respect to the manuscript (Conflict of interest, p. 7).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the Department of Hepatology, Rigshospitalet, Copenhagen; the National Institute of Public Health, University of Southern Denmark; and the Danish Cancer Society Research Center, Copenhagen, which hosts the Diet, Cancer and Health cohort (one author is credited with the acquisition of data). No industry ties are stated.

what_would_settle_it: Cohorts that measure amount and frequency repeatedly during follow-up (diaries or biomarkers of recent drinking), analysed with time-varying exposure and fine-grained adjustment for amount within frequency groups, in several populations and with enough women, using an outcome that does not depend on the clinician's knowledge of drinking (all cirrhosis with a recorded cause), would show whether frequency matters beyond amount; a cohort observing people who cut down would show whether past heavy drinking stops mattering.

domains.note: Adjusted for age, smoking, education and waist circumference only; hepatitis B and C, diabetes, diet and physical activity not adjusted. The frequency results depend on adjustment for a self-reported amount correlated with frequency (r = 0.77 and 0.85), which removed more than half of the men's age-adjusted daily-drinking excess, and the authors state the two cannot be disentangled; the wine results are open to confounding by drinking with meals and social position. For the amount gradient alone, confounding would be a smaller concern.

One self-report at baseline for a 15-year follow-up; intake in earlier decades recalled at age 50 to 64, so error grows with the distance of the period, which would by itself weaken the associations of the earlier periods; the 50–59 period overlaps the baseline measure; 236 people with conflicting answers were excluded. The judgment is driven by the life-period and frequency comparisons; current amount alone would be some concerns.

35% response, possibly healthier participants, lower than expected incidence in women; prevalent alcoholic cirrhosis excluded at baseline; 598 participants missing from the analysed cohort without explanation.
Changes in drinking during follow-up, including after early liver disease or medical advice, were not measured; baseline exposure is assumed constant.
About 1% excluded for missing covariates or inconsistent answers; register follow-up nearly complete (2 lost, 337 censored at emigration).

Register diagnoses of alcoholic cirrhosis, said to be valid; but the label 'alcoholic' requires known drinking, so classification depends on exposure (no lifetime abstainer can have the outcome, and recognised heavy or daily drinkers are more likely to be coded alcoholic). A supplementary analysis adding unspecified cirrhosis reportedly agreed (supplement not on file).

Three hypotheses stated in advance in the Introduction but no registered protocol; several adjustment levels and parametrizations; the heaviest categories and most wine-share estimates only in figures; key tables in supplements; one text value differs from its table.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The amount gradient is large, consistent in both sexes and robust to the measured confounders, and the cohort has near-complete register follow-up. The paper's own contributions, about frequency, recent against past intake and wine, rest on correlated single-occasion self-reports, recalled intake over decades, a small number of cases in women and an outcome whose definition depends on drinking; confounding by amount and measurement error are serious for each of them, so the overall risk of bias is high for those results. Citable for the association of baseline amount with alcoholic cirrhosis in middle-aged Danes and, as an association that may reflect amount, for the higher hazard in men who drank daily; not citable for advice on frequency or beverage, for the effect of cutting down, or for zero risk in lifetime abstainers.

key_findings.finding: Cohort and follow-up: 160,725 invited (December 1993 to May 1997), 27,178 men and 29,875 women took part (35%); after exclusions 55,917 were analysed; follow-up to 31 December 2011 gave 831,285 person-years (median 14.9 years); 342 developed alcoholic cirrhosis, 337 emigrated, 2 were lost and 8132 died of other causes. Incidence of alcoholic cirrhosis was 66 per 100,000 person-years in men (257 cases) and 19 in women (85 cases).

key_findings.finding: Drinking frequency was highly correlated with baseline amount (Spearman r = 0.77 in men, 0.85 in women). Median weekly amount in 12-g drinks: men drinking two to four days a week 8.9 (5th–95th percentile 3.6–13), daily 26 (9.4–60); women 6.6 (3.0–19) and 19 (7.3–40). Current abstainers' lifetime average ranged from 0.20 to 71 drinks a week in men and 0.30 to 36 in women (5th–95th percentiles).
key_findings.note: Table 1 gives current abstainers a median lifetime average of 18 drinks a week in men (higher than the 15 of daily drinkers) and 1.9 in women; 55% of male and 49% of female current abstainers smoked.

Current abstainers: men 7.58 (3.39–16.9), women 3.21 (0.77–13.4). Estimates for men drinking 42–56, 56–70 and more than 70 drinks a week, and for women above 42, appear only in Fig. 1.

key_findings.finding: No case of alcoholic cirrhosis occurred among lifetime abstainers: 63 men with 926 person-years and 265 women with 3920 person-years.
key_findings.locator: Results › Alcohol amount, 1st paragraph (p. 3); Table 2, Lifetime abstainers column (p. 4)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: at the cohort's overall rates (66 and 19 per 100,000 person-years) about 0.6 cases would be expected among the men and 0.75 among the women, and the exact Poisson upper 95% limits for zero cases are about 398 and 94 per 100,000 person-years, above the cohort averages; zero cases therefore does not show zero or lower risk. An alcoholic-cirrhosis diagnosis also presupposes a drinking history.

key_findings.finding: Wine share, men only: among men drinking 14–28 drinks a week, HR 7.47 (95% CI 1.68–33.12) with less than 1% of intake as wine, 3.12 (1.53–6.39) with 1–15% and 1.69 (0.79–3.65) with 50–100%, all against men drinking fewer than 14 drinks a week who took 50–100% of it as wine; the interaction between wine share and amount was not significant (P = 0.63). Too few cases for the analysis in women. In models controlling for other beverages, the hazard per weekly amount was lower for wine than for other beverages in men and women drinking more than 14 drinks a week (Supplementary Table 6, not on file).

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: only 35% of invitees took part and participants may be healthier; women's incidence was somewhat lower than expected from national data; self-reported intake may be under-reported, especially by women; few cases in women; deaths were only 11% of cases, too few to separate morbidity from mortality; hepatitis C status was not available.

key_findings.finding: The authors' implications: there seems to be some gain in cutting down regardless of a high lifetime intake, and "daily drinkers should be advised to drink less frequently"; they also limit the lower risk with wine to weekly amounts up to about 28–35 drinks.

key_findings.note: Quoted because the strength of the advice is at issue; no change of drinking was observed in the study.

reporting_issues.issue: 27,178 men and 29,875 women took part and seven exclusions are listed (86, 105, 27, 27, 50, 236 and 7), but 55,917 were analysed (26,696 men and 29,221 women in Table 1), fewer than the exclusions explain. Editors' arithmetic: 57,053 participants minus 538 listed exclusions leaves 56,515, so 598 participants are unaccounted for.
reporting_issues.consequence: Small (about 1% of the cohort) and unlikely to change the estimates, but the flow of participants cannot be reconstructed.
reporting_issues.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Askgaard_2015_DrinkingPatternCirrhosisCohort.pdf (online-first article in press; all text read; Table 1 checked on the rendered page)

reporting_issues.issue: For women drinking one day a week, the text gives a fully adjusted HR of 0.73 (95% CI 0.27–2.01), whereas Table 2 gives 0.81 (0.29–2.24) for the fully adjusted model and 0.73 (0.27–2.01) for the age-adjusted model.
reporting_issues.consequence: The text repeats the age-adjusted value; claims should use the table's 0.81.
reporting_issues.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Askgaard_2015_DrinkingPatternCirrhosisCohort.pdf (online-first article in press; all text read; Table 2 checked on the rendered page)

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 prints the age of men drinking two to four days a week as '55 (51-4)' and their waist circumference as '95 (81-148)', a 95th percentile far above the 112–117 cm of every other group.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical errors in descriptive data (presumably 51–64 and a smaller upper value); no effect on the hazard ratios.
reporting_issues.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Askgaard_2015_DrinkingPatternCirrhosisCohort.pdf (online-first article in press; Table 1 checked on the rendered page)

reporting_issues.issue: The text describes the interaction tests as between drinking frequency and alcoholic cirrhosis; what was tested, per the methods, is whether the per-drink slopes differ across frequency groups, that is, an interaction between frequency and amount.
reporting_issues.consequence: Wording slip; the tests concern effect modification of amount by frequency.
reporting_issues.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Askgaard_2015_DrinkingPatternCirrhosisCohort.pdf (online-first article in press; all text read)

reporting_issues.issue: Footnote 2 of Table 4 says the four life-period amounts were mutually adjusted in the first column, yet all four keep similar, significant per-drink hazard ratios (men 1.02–1.04), and the text presents that column as the association of each period before adjustment for baseline intake; it is not clear whether each row comes from one joint model or from separate models.
reporting_issues.consequence: The reader cannot tell how much each period's estimate is independent of the others; the conclusion that earlier decades do not matter rests on the second column, where baseline intake is added.
reporting_issues.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Askgaard_2015_DrinkingPatternCirrhosisCohort.pdf (online-first article in press; all text read; Table 4 checked on the rendered page)

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives the wine comparison as against drinking fewer than 14 drinks a week, but the reference group is men drinking fewer than 14 drinks a week who took 50–100% of it as wine.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's hazard ratios cannot be read as against light drinkers in general.
reporting_issues.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Askgaard_2015_DrinkingPatternCirrhosisCohort.pdf (online-first article in press; all text read)

reporting_issues.issue: The text says that adjustment for smoking, education and waist circumference altered the estimates only a little, but in Table 2 it moved men's HR for less than one day a week from 0.89 to 1.34 and for daily drinking from 4.83 to 3.65, and women's for current abstainers from 6.14 to 4.03.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the measured confounders changed some estimates by a quarter or more, which makes residual confounding by unmeasured factors more plausible, not less.
reporting_issues.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Askgaard_2015_DrinkingPatternCirrhosisCohort.pdf (online-first article in press; all text read; Table 2 checked on the rendered page)

editorial_corrections.to: Roerecke et al. (Am J Gastroenterol), dose–response meta-analysis of alcohol and cirrhosis (card sc_roerecke_2019): this cohort is one of its nine studies (its Table 1), although the cohort's men contribute no estimate to its main analysis. It reports daily-drinking ratios for this cohort at the same weekly intake (men 2.25, women 1.28) that are not in this paper's main text, which gives 3.65 and 1.73 (Table 2, fully adjusted).
editorial_corrections.reason: Update: the 2019 review now has a reference record and a card; its card lists the Diet, Cancer and Health cohort among its primary studies and records that the cohort's men contribute no estimate. The differing ratios were found by AI reader 172 (claim writer) and checked by the editor against this paper's Table 2 (p. 4 of the online-first PDF).
Links the entry to the reference record now built.

editorial_corrections.from: The steep amount gradient agrees with the meta-analyses (sc_rehm_2010). The association of daily drinking with alcoholic cirrhosis in men agrees in direction with earlier clinical studies the authors cite, but in this cohort it cannot be separated from amount, and in women it was not found; the wine finding agrees with one earlier Danish study and conflicts with studies of heavy drinkers. The Diet, Cancer and Health cohort is not among the 17 studies of Rehm et al. (2010), so the two are independent; overlap with the 2019 meta-analysis must be checked before both are cited for one claim.
editorial_corrections.to: The steep amount gradient agrees with the meta-analyses (sc_rehm_2010). The association of daily drinking with alcoholic cirrhosis in men agrees in direction with earlier clinical studies the authors cite, but in this cohort it cannot be separated from amount, and in women it was not found; the wine finding agrees with one earlier Danish study and conflicts with studies of heavy drinkers. The Diet, Cancer and Health cohort is not among the 17 studies of Rehm et al. (2010), so the two are independent; the 2019 meta-analysis (Roerecke et al.) includes this cohort, so the two are not independent and are counted once when cited together.
editorial_corrections.reason: Follows the update above: the overlap is now checked.
